doc.title: Cascadu interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019

chapter: Spirit, roots and the music's meaning
title: Touching lives; Trinidad carnival brass bands; tolerance
summary: Cascadu reflects on the gift of touching lives, the loss of carnival brass bands, and tolerance toward other players.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: And they live it. We live it. And I’m fortunate, I feel really really blessed at this stage in my life to be doing something like what we did yesterday in the performance and performing with other people etcetera, and being able to touch lives. You know I remember, you know, in Trinidad we had, part of the carnival culture was to have these huge brass bands on the road. And I had belonged to one of the big and really hot brass bands back in the 80s into the early 90s in Trinidad. And it shaped the lives of so many younger musicians. And it was sad to hear that, you know, they didn’t have those brass bands, like the DJs took over and now they didn’t want to pay musicians. They could have DJs and people making some noise and stuff, and you know everybody’s going down the street and the bands just got wiped out completely. And it was — I was happy to hear a young musician saying recently that he is trying to revive this because his musicianship, his love for music, came from hearing these big brass bands on the road during carnival, and he wanted to play his trumpet. He wanted to be part of that section you know. And where we go today and where we play today, you have no idea of whose life you are going to touch and in what way you’re going to touch that life. And that’s a gift that we have been given. It’s a gift that we have to nurture. It’s a gift that we have to respect. It’s a gift that we have to hold in the highest elevation because that is our purpose.
Do you get aggravated if you’re playing, you’re thrown together with other percussionists or that are playing this music, and they don’t treat it with the same respect or passion that you do?

I don’t. Because I recognize that everybody is coming from a different place you know. There is tolerance and there is leading by example. And I’ve always believed that if your character and if your composure can speak for you in what it is you are doing then somehow or the other you’re going to touch that life and people are going to remember and take something with you. And it doesn’t matter what they take as long as they take something with you and it helps to transform their lives or their thinking or their thought down the road. “Okay. Take a piece of me.” You know? Even if you’re not a musician
